text: March, eighteen ninety-four. Pelican Valley, deep in Yellowstone's backcountry. The snow is deep, the wind is hard, and an Army scout named Felix Burgess is following a trail of snowshoe tracks.

Most members of Congress had never seen anything like Yellowstone. Jackson's photographs and Moran's watercolor sketches showed them a place that looked unreal: boiling springs, a golden canyon, waterfalls. On March first, eighteen seventy-two, President Ulysses S. Grant signed a law making Yellowstone the world's first national park, as the idea is understood today.

You may have heard how the idea was born. In eighteen seventy, explorers sat around a campfire right here, at the meeting of two rivers, and one of them proposed that the land should belong to everyone. It's a great story. It probably never happened. About twenty firsthand accounts of that expedition survive, and not one of them mentions it. The story first appeared in print more than thirty years later.

So people did whatever they wanted. In one winter alone, hunters killed some three thousand elk in and around the park, just for their hides. Tourists broke off pieces of geyser cones as souvenirs, and threw logs and junk into geysers just to see what would happen.

In eighteen seventy-seven, a new superintendent, [Philetus](/fɪlˈiːtəs/) Norris, took over, and the next year Congress finally gave him a salary and some money. He built a log blockhouse headquarters on a hill above Mammoth, and he built roads. Parts of his route still form the Grand Loop you drive today. He hired a tough mountain man named Harry [Yount](/jˈaʊnt/) as the park's first gamekeeper, often called the first park ranger.

But Norris had no real power to arrest anyone. There was no law to enforce. Norris was pushed out in eighteen eighty-two. And in eighteen eighty-six, Congress stopped paying anyone to run the park at all.

On August seventeenth, eighteen eighty-six, Captain Moses Harris rode into Mammoth with fifty men of the First U.S. Cavalry. His new office was a broken-down blacksmith shop. Army engineer Hiram Chittenden, who wrote the park's first history, later called Harris "vigorous and uncompromising in suppressing lawlessness."
Harris didn't waste time. He threw out rule-breakers, stopped livestock from grazing near the park's wonders, and posted soldiers at the most famous sights.

Soldiers lived in small stations across the park, sixteen of them by the end. In summer they patrolled on horseback. In winter, they patrolled on skis, sometimes twenty miles a day, sleeping in small backcountry cabins and hunting for poachers' tracks in the snow. Civilian Army scouts went with them. Some of their diaries still survive in the park's archives.

By luck, a writer named Emerson Hough was in the park that winter, on an expedition with the official park photographer, F. Jay Haynes. Hough sent word of the capture to his editor, George Bird Grinnell, at the magazine Forest and Stream.

On August twenty-fourth, nineteen-oh-eight, a few miles past Kepler Cascades, on the road between Old Faithful and West Thumb, a single masked man stepped out of the trees. One by one, he stopped the coaches as they came around the bend. By the most-cited count, he robbed seventeen of them, more than a hundred and seventy passengers. He was never caught.
They left something behind. The ranger's famous flat hat traces its roots to the wide-brimmed campaign hats of the Army.

And in the summer of eighteen seventy-seven, just five years after the park was created, as many as eight hundred [Nez Perce](/nˌɛz pˈɜɹs/) men, women and children crossed Yellowstone, running from the U.S. Army. That's the next chapter. See you there.
